notes.meaning: The women went to the tomb at daybreak to finish burying Jesus with prepared spices, showing their deep love for Him. Because Jesus rose on this morning, the first day of the week became the regular day Christians gather to worship. Their early arrival also shows they were not expecting a resurrection, but came simply to care for His dead body.

When the women arrived, they saw the heavy entrance stone had already been rolled aside. An angel had moved the stone, not to let Jesus out, but to let witnesses look inside. Any obstacle they worried about along the way had already been cleared away by God.

The women stepped inside the tomb and discovered that the body of the Lord Jesus was gone. The Gospels do not describe the moment of the resurrection itself, but only the quiet fact of the empty tomb. His holy body had not been stolen or hidden, but had been raised from death.

As the women stood there confused and upset, two angels appeared before them looking like men in shining, radiant clothes. Their bright garments reflected the pure glory and holiness of heaven. Just as angels announced Jesus's birth to humble shepherds, angels now announced His rising to faithful women.

Overwhelmed by holy fear and reverence, the women bowed down to the ground. The angels gently asked why they were searching for the living Lord in a place meant only for the dead. Jesus is the living One who can never be held by the grave or found among dead things.

The angels declared the great good news: Jesus was not in the grave because He had risen. They told the women to remember what Jesus had told them back in Galilee. The resurrection was not an unexpected accident, but the exact fulfillment of what the Lord had promised.

The angels quoted Jesus's own reminder that He had to be handed over to sinful men, die on a cross, and rise on the third day. This plan was necessary to rescue people from sin according to God's purpose. The third day had now arrived, counting Friday as the first day and Sunday as the third.

Hearing the angels' reminder, the women suddenly recalled Jesus's own teachings. His words had been stored in their memories, and God's message brought them back to mind with new understanding. Remembering what Jesus said turned their confusion into comforting hope.

The women quickly left the tomb and hurried to tell everything they had seen to the eleven apostles and the other disciples. God honored their quiet loyalty by making them the very first messengers of the resurrection. They delivered their report with a mixture of wonder, joy, and holy awe.

Luke names some of the women who carried this news, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James. Joanna was the wife of King Herod's household manager, showing that women of different backgrounds supported Jesus. By recording their names, Luke highlights real eyewitnesses who stood by Jesus to the end.

The apostles thought the women were talking nonsense, like people delirious with fever, and refused to believe them. The disciples were so crushed by the cross that they had completely given up hope. Their stubborn doubt actually shows they did not make up the resurrection story out of wishful thinking.

Peter jumped up and ran to the tomb to see for himself what had happened. Peering inside, he saw only the linen burial cloths lying neatly without the body. He walked away puzzled and wondering, because he had not yet connected the empty tomb with Jesus's promise to rise.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient Greek manuscripts leave out this verse, leading some textual critics to view it as an addition borrowed from John's Gospel, though many scholars regard it as genuine.

notes.meaning: Later that same day, two of Jesus's followers were walking to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. These travelers were ordinary disciples rather than members of the eleven apostles. They were likely heading home after keeping the Passover feast in the city.

As they walked the dusty road, the two friends talked over everything that had taken place during the weekend. Their minds were filled with grief over Jesus's arrest, trial, and shameful crucifixion. Sharing their thoughts helped them process the heavy sorrow weighing on their hearts.

While they debated the meaning of these strange events, Jesus Himself came up and began walking alongside them. He came as an ordinary traveler, joining their journey quietly. When believers talk honestly about the Lord, He often draws near to help and comfort them.

Even though Jesus was right beside them, the two disciples were kept from recognizing who He was. God shielded their vision so that Jesus could first instruct them through the Scriptures before revealing His identity. Their own deep sorrow and lack of expectation also clouded their awareness.

Jesus asked them what serious matter they were debating back and forth as they walked. At His question, they stopped in their tracks, their faces dark with sadness. The Lord asked not because He lacked knowledge, but to invite them to open their hearts freely.

Cleopas answered in surprise, asking if this traveler was the only visitor in Jerusalem who had not heard what happened. The public execution of Jesus had caused such a stir that it seemed impossible for any pilgrim to miss it. Cleopas could not imagine anyone in the area being unaware of the weekend's events.

Jesus asked them to explain, and they described Jesus of Nazareth as a mighty prophet in both preaching and miracles before God and all the people. They still held Him in deep honor as a true teacher sent from God. Yet calling Him only a prophet showed that their faith in Him as the promised Messiah had been shaken.

They explained how their own chief priests and Jewish rulers handed Jesus over to be condemned to death and crucified. The Jewish leaders instigated the charges and demanded the sentence from the Roman governor. For these followers, seeing their respected leaders condemn Jesus was a shocking blow.

Cleopas confessed that they had hoped Jesus was the Messiah who would redeem Israel by freeing them from foreign rule. Instead, He was dead, and it was already the third day since His crucifixion. Their words reveal a broken heart and confused mind, still clinging to a tiny spark of hope on the day Jesus had promised something might happen.

Cleopas added that some women from their company had startled them with an astonishing report early that morning. The women had gone to the tomb at dawn, expecting to find a dead body. Instead, their unexpected news had thrown the whole group into utter amazement.

The women reported that Jesus's body was missing and that angels had appeared telling them Jesus was alive. To the two disciples, this seemed almost too good to be true and sounded like an uncertain vision. They could hardly trust such surprising news while their hearts were still crushed by grief.

Some of their companions, including Peter and John, then hurried to the tomb and found it empty, exactly as the women said. Yet because they did not actually see Jesus Himself, their doubts remained. An empty grave alone was not enough to convince them that their Lord was truly alive.

Jesus gently rebuked them for being foolish and slow of heart to believe what the Old Testament prophets had written. He was not insulting their intelligence, but pointing out their spiritual blindness and hesitation to trust God's word. They had readily believed the promises of a glorious King, but overlooked the prophecies of a suffering servant.

Jesus asked if the Messiah did not have to suffer all these things before entering into His heavenly glory. His death was not a defeat or a tragic mistake, but God's required way to pay for sins and fulfill the Scriptures. The very cross that caused their doubts was actually proof that He is the true Messiah.
